results.result: The authors developed and validated a novel parasagittal somatosensory corticostriatal slice preparation containing ~8 whisker barrels with preserved projections from barrel cortex to DLS. LSPS with glutamate uncaging excited cortical neurons within 75 µm of their soma on 2.8±0.3 grid sites, evoked monosynaptic EPSCs of 40±1 pA amplitude consistent with 1-5 presynaptic cells per connected site, and resulted in <10% estimated loss of S1 inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C27 and C122 provide converging anatomical, electrophysiological, and computational evidence validating the slice preparation. The biocytin labeling (C21), spatial resolution of glutamate uncaging (C23-C24), monosynaptic nature of responses (C25), EPSC amplitudes (C26-C27), and modeling of input loss (C122) collectively demonstrate that the preparation preserves functional connectivity while enabling precise mapping. The consistency with prior anatomical studies (C35) further supports validity.

results.result: Layer 5a is the primary source of cortical innervation to SPNs, with ~65% of SPNs receiving L5a input. L5a dominance is due to higher connectivity probability rather than stronger synapses, as EPSC amplitudes were similar across L2/3-L5b but smaller in L6. Some apparent L4 connectivity reflects activation of nearby L5a cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C35 and C88 provide consistent evidence for L5a as the primary input source. The quantitative connectivity data (C28), control experiments distinguishing direct L2/3 connections from L5a activation (C29-C31), similar EPSC amplitudes across layers except L6 (C32, C34), and consistency with prior anatomical studies (C35, C88) collectively support this conclusion. The inference about connectivity probability vs. synaptic strength (C33) is well-justified by the data.

results.result: The corticostriatal projection exhibits asymmetric convergence and divergence: cortical inputs to SPNs span 2.5 mm in barrel cortex while SPNs occupy only 1 mm in striatum, whereas individual cortical columns (~150 µm) project to SPNs distributed across ~600 µm of striatum. This implies overlapping functional projections from adjacent cortical columns in the DLS.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 describe complementary aspects of projection organization supported by quantitative measurements from connectivity maps. The convergence (C36) and divergence (C37) measurements are internally consistent and lead to the logical inference of overlapping projections (C38) that is further supported by consistency with prior anatomical studies. The asymmetry is a key feature enabling subsequent analyses of convergence.

results.result: Individual SPNs receive sparse, discontinuous cortical input organized in 1-6 clusters (average 1.9) spanning 1-8 cortical columns (average 2.7). Clusters are typically one column wide (171±7 µm), separated by gaps of 265±28 µm, resulting in input fields of 535±42 µm width with connectivity gaps comprising ~45% of the horizontal extent. 60% of SPNs responded to stimulation of only 1-2 whisker cortical columns.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15, C39-C44, C46, and C89 provide comprehensive quantitative characterization of sparse connectivity patterns. The measurements are internally consistent (cluster number, width, spacing, and resulting input field dimensions), and the finding that connectivity gaps comprise substantial portions of input fields (C46) directly supports the conclusion of sparse, discontinuous innervation. The quantification that 60% of SPNs respond to only 1-2 columns (C89) provides strong evidence for low convergence.

results.result: The sparse connectivity patterns are genuine features of corticostriatal organization rather than artifacts of slice preparation, as SPNs with small and large input fields are intermingled in the striatum, input field width shows no correlation with SPN position (R=0.05, p=0.61), and SPNs receiving input from single columns coexist with multi-column SPNs in the same slice.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 provide multiple lines of evidence ruling out systematic artifacts. The lack of spatial organization of input field sizes (C47-C48), absence of correlation with recording position (C48-C49), and coexistence of different connectivity patterns in the same slice (C50) collectively demonstrate that sparse connectivity is not due to edge effects or incomplete preservation of projections. This validation is critical for interpreting the main findings.

results.result: Individual SPNs receive inputs distributed across 2.4±0.1 cortical layers on average, with 55% of cortical columns innervating SPNs through projections from a single layer. This suggests that presynaptic neurons are dispersed such that inputs may originate from distinct layers as well as different whisker columns.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 characterize the vertical organization of connectivity. The quantitative measurements (C51-C52) support the inference that inputs are dispersed across both horizontal and vertical dimensions (C53). This finding complements the horizontal sparsity analysis and contributes to the overall picture of selective connectivity.

results.result: Neighboring SPNs have distinct connectivity patterns with minimal redundancy. While 77% of SPN pairs <100 µm apart have overlapping input fields, only 18±2% of connected sites are vertically aligned and only 7.7±1.6% overlap. Shared connectivity occurs only for SPNs <250 µm apart, whereas input fields overlap up to 500 µm separation, indicating that distant SPNs can share cortical regions without sharing presynaptic neurons in the same column.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C54-C60, C104-C107 provide comprehensive paired analysis demonstrating local heterogeneity. The quantitative measurements show clear distance-dependent effects with distinct thresholds for input field overlap vs. connected site overlap (C55-C56, C105-C106). The low percentages of alignment and overlap even for neighboring cells (C57-C58) strongly support the conclusion of minimal redundancy (C59-C60, C104). The inference about shared regions without shared neurons (C107) logically follows from the data.

results.result: Despite sparse individual connectivity, the projection exhibits loose topographic organization at the population level: SPNs located laterally/medially in striatum have connectivity centers of mass in lateral/medial barrel cortex. However, adjacent SPNs can have connectivity centers 1 mm apart, indicating less precise topography than intracortical projections. The connectivity model is selective, broad, and loosely topographic.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 demonstrate population-level organization despite individual sparsity. The correlation between SPN position and connectivity center of mass (C61-C62) establishes topography, while the large variability between adjacent cells (C63) and comparison to intracortical projections (C64) appropriately qualify the precision. The synthesis into a connectivity model (C65) is well-supported by the combined findings. This reconciles apparent contradictions between sparse individual connectivity and known anatomical topography.

results.result: EPSC amplitudes are heterogeneous within input maps but show no consistent spatial pattern relative to connectivity centers of mass. Connectivity CM and synaptic input CM (weighted by EPSC amplitude) yield nearly identical correlations with SPN position (R=0.60 vs 0.62, p=0.98), with synaptic input CMs shifted only 45±5 µm from connectivity CMs. This confirms connectivity patterns, not synaptic strength gradients, as principal determinants of topographic organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 test whether synaptic strength contributes to topographic organization. The statistical comparison (C67), small shift in centers of mass (C68), and lack of consistent spatial pattern (C69) provide strong evidence that connectivity patterns dominate. The conclusion (C70) is well-justified and important for understanding the mechanisms of topographic organization.

results.result: In SPNs with multiple clusters, the strongest cluster provides 1.12-55 times more input than other clusters (average 6.8±1.4-fold), suggesting that despite multi-column innervation, some SPNs may still exhibit preference for particular whisker columns due to heterogeneity between clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 quantify cluster strength heterogeneity and draw a reasonable inference about functional implications. The large range and average dominance (C71) support the speculation about whisker selectivity (C72), which is appropriately qualified as a possibility. This finding helps reconcile the anatomical observation of multi-column innervation with prior in vivo observations of whisker selectivity.

results.result: D1 and D2 SPNs have similar connectivity patterns: input field widths, number of cortical columns, cluster widths, laminar distribution, total input strength, and cluster dominance do not differ between subtypes. Paired analysis of D1 and D2 SPNs in the same slice confirms these similarities. The heterogeneity in innervation patterns is not due to differences between SPN subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C73-C81 provide comprehensive comparison of D1 and D2 SPNs across multiple connectivity metrics. The consistency of findings across unpaired (C75-C76, C78, C80-C81) and paired analyses (C77), combined with appropriate identification of D2 SPNs based on prior literature (C73), strongly support the conclusion of similar connectivity patterns (C79). This is an important negative result that constrains models of pathway-specific connectivity.

results.result: Despite similar overall connectivity patterns, D1 and D2 SPNs show layer-specific differences in synaptic strength: L2/3-EPSCT is larger in D2 SPNs (132±36 vs 53±22 pA, p=0.005) while L6-EPSCT is larger in D1 SPNs (37±10 vs 16±2 pA, p=0.038). Single-site EPSC analysis indicates these differences arise from differential synaptic strength rather than connectivity probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C19, C82-C87 identify layer-specific differences with appropriate statistical testing. The total EPSCT measurements (C83-C84) are supported by single-site EPSC analysis (C85-C86), which justifies the mechanistic inference about synaptic strength (C87). The specificity to L2/3 and L6 while L5 is similar (C82) is an important detail. These findings reveal pathway-specific differences in synaptic properties despite similar connectivity patterns.

results.result: The high convergence of somatosensory inputs to striatum is accomplished through sparse yet complementary connectivity to individual SPNs. Within a loosely topographic organization, each SPN integrates limited and heterogeneous rather than exhaustive inputs from barrel cortex. The speckled connectivity pattern suggests synapses are established through a selective and/or competitive process.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C60, C99-C100 synthesize the main findings into an overall model. The conclusion of sparse yet complementary connectivity (C20, C99) is well-supported by the extensive characterization of individual sparsity (Results 4-5) and local heterogeneity (Result 7). The inference about selective/competitive synapse formation (C100) is appropriately presented as a suggestion rather than a proven mechanism. This represents the central conceptual advance of the paper.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence support that sparse innervation is genuine rather than artifactual: (i) slice orientation captures the axis of greatest axonal overlap; (ii) peak connectivity is with L5a as expected; (iii) connected sites span broad axes implying preserved intervening projections; (iv) adjacent SPNs have different patterns in the same slice; (v) connectivity clusters are sparser in larger input fields; (vi) small EPSCs consistent with few presynaptic cells per site.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 provide six independent arguments validating the main findings. Each argument addresses a potential artifact or alternative explanation. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence (anatomical orientation, layer specificity, spatial distribution, local heterogeneity, scaling relationships, and EPSC amplitudes) provides strong support for the conclusion that sparse connectivity is a genuine biological feature. This validation is essential for the paper's conclusions.

results.result: The potential loss of distal dendritic inputs due to slice preparation is estimated to be minimal (<10%) based on modeling, as 80% of S1 synaptic contacts are distributed along dendrites but distal synapses are proportionally rare.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 address a key methodological concern about incomplete sampling of inputs. The modeling approach (C92) appropriately incorporates anatomical data about synapse distribution (C90-C91) to estimate input loss. The <10% estimate provides quantitative support that the main findings are not substantially affected by this limitation. However, the modeling assumptions and implementation details are not fully described, introducing some uncertainty.

results.result: The observation that SPNs must be <250 µm apart to share inputs was not predicted by prior ultrastructural models, which suggested that two SPNs would be more likely to share cortical inputs if their dendrites extended into different striatal subregions (due to sparse bouton distribution). The current findings contradict this prediction.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103, C108-C109 compare current findings to prior theoretical predictions. The description of the Wilson model (C101-C103) and its predictions (C109) are appropriately cited, and the observation that current findings contradict these predictions (C108) is well-supported by the distance-dependent overlap data (Result 7). This represents an important advance in understanding corticostriatal connectivity principles.

results.result: A possible explanation for shared connectivity in nearby SPNs is that they are innervated by different neurons co-localized in barrel cortex (<75 µm apart). Such events could explain striatal clusters observed in vivo where neurons have similar but non-identical sensory selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 propose speculative explanations for observed patterns. While the hypothesis about co-localized presynaptic neurons (C110) is plausible given the spatial resolution of the technique (75 µm), it is not directly tested. The connection to in vivo clustering (C111) is reasonable but also speculative. These are appropriate hypotheses for future work but lack direct experimental support in the current study.

results.result: The authors propose that a complete representation of whiskers could emerge at the population level with each SPN's representation complementing its neighbors, that the observations suggest a selective or competitive process underlying synapse formation, and that input convergence could be modulated by plasticity enabling experience-driven reconfiguration.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 present speculative models and hypotheses for future investigation. While these are reasonable interpretations of the findings, they lack direct experimental support in the current study. The population-level representation model (C119) is a logical inference from the complementary connectivity patterns, but the mechanisms of selective/competitive synapse formation (C120) and plasticity-driven reconfiguration (C121) are not tested. These represent appropriate directions for future work but should not be considered supported conclusions.

results.result: The authors discuss prior findings that D1 SPNs show larger responses than D2 SPNs to whisker deflections and cortical stimulation, validate that L2/3 and L6 stimulation activates only those respective projections, and speculate about functional implications of differential L2/3 and L6 inputs to D1 vs D2 SPNs based on the known roles of these layers in sensory processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C118 provide context from prior literature (C112-C113, C117-C118) and validate the interpretation of layer-specific stimulation (C114-C115). The speculation about functional implications (C116) is appropriately qualified and grounded in cited literature about layer function. This discussion appropriately contextualizes the layer-specific differences found in Result 12 and suggests functional significance, though the functional claims themselves are not tested.

results.result: The authors developed and validated a novel parasagittal somatosensory corticostriatal slice preparation containing approximately 8 whisker barrels with preserved projections from barrel cortex to DLS. The LSPS method was validated to excite cortical neurons within 75 μm, activate 2.8±0.3 grid sites on average, and elicit monosynaptic EPSCs while preventing feedforward inhibition, with estimated loss of S1 inputs <10%.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly praised the methodology. Reviewer 3 stated 'The authors developed and validated a novel slice preparation' and 'The use of a novel ex vivo slice prep that keeps relevant corticostriatal projections intact allows for careful mapping.' Reviewer 2 noted 'The methodology shows impressive rigor' and Reviewer 1 stated 'The experiments were well-designed and conducted.' No concerns were raised about the slice preparation or LSPS validation.

results.result: Individual SPNs received sparse, clustered cortical input organized in 1-6 clusters (average 1.9±0.1) from a small number of whisker cortical columns (60% from only 1-2 columns). Clusters were approximately one column wide (171±7 μm), separated by substantial gaps (265±28 μm average), with input field widths ranging 0.075-1.6 mm (average 535±42 μm) that remained constant across SPN positions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously accepted these findings as core results. The editor stated the evidence is 'compelling, demonstrating that SPNs uniquely integrate sparse input from variable stretches across the barrel cortex.' Reviewer 3 noted 'They found that individual SPNs were driven by sparse, scattered cortical clusters' and 'the major claims are well-supported.' Reviewer 2 stated 'the data robustly support the authors conclusions.'

results.result: Neighboring SPNs had distinct, cell-specific connectivity patterns with minimal redundancy. While 77% of neighboring SPNs (<100 μm apart) had overlapping input fields, only 7.7±1.6% of their connected sites actually overlapped, and alignment occurred only when SPNs were <300 μm apart. Input fields continued to intersect up to 500 μm separation, but without shared presynaptic partners.
results.evaluation: This finding was explicitly highlighted by reviewers as a key result. Reviewer 3 stated 'while the cortical input fields of nearby SPNs had some degree of overlap, connectivity per SPN was largely distinct' and noted this was 'Interestingly' demonstrated. The editor emphasized 'SPNs uniquely integrate sparse input' as a fundamental finding. No concerns were raised about these paired analyses.

results.result: Despite sparse individual connectivity, the projection showed loose topographic organization at the population level, with SPN position in striatum correlating with connectivity center of mass in barrel cortex (R=0.60, p<0.001). The topography was less precise than intracortical projections, with adjacent SPNs' connectivity centers potentially 1 mm apart. EPSC amplitudes did not alter this topographic relationship (R=0.62 for synaptic input CM vs. 0.60 for connectivity CM).
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly stated this as a fundamental finding: 'inputs from discrete whisker cortical columns are convergent and SPN-specific, but topographically organized at the population level.' Reviewer 3 noted 'Despite sparse, heterogeneous connectivity, topographical organization was identified.' All reviewers accepted this as a well-supported conclusion with no concerns raised.

results.result: Layer 5a was the primary source of cortical innervation, with ~65% of SPNs receiving L5a input, primarily due to higher connectivity probability rather than stronger synapses. L2/3 stimulation activated only L2/3 projections (never L5a cells), while 50% of L5a cells fired when L4 bottom was stimulated. EPSCs from L2/3-L5b had similar amplitudes, but L6-EPSCs were significantly smaller. Individual SPNs received input from 2.4±0.1 cortical layers on average.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly noted 'Careful reporting of both columnar and layer position' as a strength. The editor and reviewers accepted these layer-specific findings without question. Reviewer 3 stated the study 'allows the authors to uncover novel details' about representation, implicitly accepting the layer analysis. No concerns were raised about the laminar connectivity patterns.

results.result: D1 and D2 SPNs showed similar overall connectivity patterns, with no differences in input field width, number of cortical columns innervating them, cluster widths, layer proportions, total EPSC sum, or dominance of principal clusters. The heterogeneity in innervation patterns was not due to differences between SPN subtypes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly stated 'The authors lastly compared direct (D1) vs. indirect (D2) pathway cells, concluding that overall connectivity patterns were the same' and noted this was carefully reported. The editor and other reviewers raised no concerns about these comparisons. The finding that D1 and D2 patterns are similar was accepted as well-supported.

results.result: Despite similar connectivity patterns, D1 and D2 SPNs showed layer-specific differences in synaptic strength. D2 SPNs received larger L2/3 inputs (L2/3-EPSCT: 132±36 vs 53±22 pA, p=0.005; single-site EPSCs: 48±11 vs 27±5 pA, p=0.043), while D1 SPNs received larger L6 inputs (L6-EPSCT: 37±10 vs 16±2 pA, p=0.038; single-site EPSCs: 24±2 vs 16±2 pA, p=0.038). L5 inputs were similar between cell types.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 stated 'D1 cells received stronger input from L6 and D2 cells from L2/3' as part of the study's conclusions. This layer-specific difference was accepted alongside the finding of similar overall patterns. No reviewer questioned these statistically significant differences or the interpretation that synaptic strength differences underlie the layer-specific effects.

results.result: EPSCs had small amplitudes (40±1 pA, n=550), consistent with only one or a few presynaptic cells (≤5) at each connected site based on comparison with known miniature EPSC amplitudes (10-20 pA).
results.evaluation: This quantitative finding was not questioned by any reviewer. Reviewer 2 stated 'the data robustly support the authors conclusions' and Reviewer 1 noted 'data analysis was thorough.' The inference about presynaptic cell numbers based on EPSC amplitudes was accepted as part of the overall evidence for sparse connectivity.

results.result: The projection showed asymmetric convergence-divergence relationships: SPNs in a 1 mm striatal region received input from a 2.5 mm cortical band, while a single cortical column (~150 μm) projected to SPNs distributed across ~600 μm of striatum. This implied that functional projections from adjacent cortical columns overlapped in the DLS.
results.evaluation: These measurements were accepted as part of the overall characterization of the projection. The editor stated the evidence is 'compelling' and reviewers noted the 'thorough analysis' (Reviewer 1) and 'rigorous functional mapping' (Reviewer 3). The consistency with known anatomy was noted in the manuscript and not challenged.

results.result: EPSC amplitudes were heterogeneous within input maps, with the strongest cluster providing 1.12-55 times greater input than other clusters (average 6.8±1.4-fold). This heterogeneity could permit some SPNs to have preference for a particular whisker cortical column despite multiple clusters.
results.evaluation: This finding was accepted as part of the detailed characterization. Reviewer 1 stated 'data analysis was thorough' and Reviewer 2 noted 'impressive rigor.' The interpretation about potential whisker preference was presented as a possibility and not challenged by reviewers.

results.result: The overall connectivity model is characterized as selective, broad, and loosely topographic, where each SPN integrates limited and heterogeneous rather than exhaustive inputs from barrel cortex. The presence of different connectivity patterns in adjacent SPNs within the same slice supports a pool of potential connections larger than actual connections, with connectivity clusters becoming sparser in larger input fields, suggesting regulated convergence.
results.evaluation: This is the main interpretive conclusion that reviewers explicitly endorsed. The editor stated 'The evidence supporting this claim is compelling' and Reviewer 3 noted 'Their results indicate selective input that is loosely topographic.' Reviewer 2 stated the manuscript 'provides valuable insights into corticostriatal architecture.' All reviewers accepted this model as well-supported by the data.

results.result: The speckled connectivity pattern suggests that somatosensory corticostriatal synapses are established through a selective and/or competitive process, with potential for plasticity-driven reconfiguration of S1 corticostriatal coupling.
results.evaluation: These are speculative mechanistic proposals about synapse formation and plasticity. While reviewers accepted the descriptive findings, they did not explicitly endorse these mechanistic interpretations. The claims are presented as suggestions and hypotheses rather than demonstrated findings, and reviewers did not comment on these speculative aspects.

results.result: The observation that SPNs must be <250 μm apart to share inputs was not predicted by prior ultrastructural models, which predicted the opposite pattern. A possible explanation is that pairs with shared connectivity were innervated by different but co-localized neurons (<75 μm apart), which could explain in vivo striatal clusters with similar but non-identical sensory selectivity.
results.evaluation: This represents a comparison with prior models and speculative explanations. While the empirical finding about the 250 μm distance threshold was accepted (part of the paired analysis), the mechanistic explanations are speculative. Reviewers did not explicitly comment on these interpretations or the comparison with Wilson's model.

results.result: The larger L2/3 inputs to D2 SPNs may be functionally significant given L2/3's role in higher-order integration and sustained responses during whisker-wall contacts. L6 diversity in corticofugal neurons relates to different behavioral states. A complete whisker representation could emerge at the population level with each SPN's representation complementing its neighbors.
results.evaluation: These are speculative functional interpretations connecting the findings to prior literature. While reviewers accepted the empirical layer-specific differences, they did not explicitly endorse these functional interpretations. The population-level representation model is presented as a possibility ('could emerge') rather than a demonstrated finding.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the slice preparation methodology and validation (C21-C25, C122). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation of anatomical and electrophysiological features. Peer reviewers unanimously praised the methodology as 'novel', 'rigorous', and 'well-designed'. Both strongly support the validity of the preparation, though OpenEval provides more granular technical justification while peer review offers broader methodological endorsement.

Both address sparse connectivity patterns (C14-C15, C39-C44, C46, C89). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative characterization of cluster properties and connectivity gaps. Peer reviewers unanimously accepted these as 'core results' with 'compelling' evidence, noting SPNs receive 'sparse, scattered cortical clusters'. Both strongly support the finding of sparse, discontinuous innervation.

Both evaluate local heterogeneity and minimal redundancy between nearby SPNs (C16, C54-C60, C104-C107). OpenEval emphasizes distance-dependent effects and quantitative overlap measurements. Peer reviewers explicitly highlighted this as a key finding, noting 'connectivity per SPN was largely distinct' despite overlapping input fields. Both strongly support the conclusion of unique, non-redundant connectivity patterns.

Both address population-level topographic organization (C61-C65, C67-C70). OpenEval details the correlation between SPN position and connectivity center of mass while noting high local variability. Peer reviewers explicitly endorsed this as 'fundamental', stating inputs are 'topographically organized at the population level' despite sparse individual connectivity. Both support the reconciliation of sparse connectivity with population topography.

Both evaluate layer-specific connectivity patterns, particularly L5a as primary input source (C28-C35, C88). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative evidence and control experiments. Peer reviewers accepted these findings, noting 'careful reporting of both columnar and layer position' as a strength. OpenEval also addresses vertical organization (C51-C53) which peer review implicitly accepts. Both support the laminar connectivity characterization.

Both evaluate D1 vs D2 SPN connectivity patterns (C18, C73-C81). OpenEval provides comprehensive comparison across multiple metrics showing similar patterns. Peer reviewers explicitly stated 'overall connectivity patterns were the same' and accepted this as carefully reported. Both support the conclusion that D1 and D2 SPNs have similar connectivity patterns despite pathway differences.

Both address layer-specific differences in synaptic strength between D1 and D2 SPNs (C19, C82-C87, C114-C115). OpenEval details statistical differences in L2/3 and L6 with mechanistic interpretation about synaptic strength. Peer reviewers stated 'D1 cells received stronger input from L6 and D2 cells from L2/3' and accepted these differences. Both support the layer-specific synaptic strength differences.

Both evaluate projection organization including convergence and divergence (C36-C38). OpenEval provides quantitative measurements and notes asymmetry enabling convergence analysis. Peer reviewers accepted these as part of 'thorough analysis' and 'rigorous functional mapping' with 'compelling' evidence. Both support the characterization of projection organization.

Both address cluster strength heterogeneity and potential whisker selectivity (C66, C71-C72). OpenEval quantifies the range and average dominance, presenting whisker selectivity as appropriately qualified speculation. Peer reviewers accepted this as part of 'thorough' and 'rigorous' analysis without challenge. Both support the quantitative finding while treating functional implications as speculative.

Both evaluate the main interpretive conclusion about sparse yet complementary connectivity (C20, C60, C99-C100). OpenEval synthesizes findings into a model with selective synapse formation as suggestion. Peer reviewers explicitly endorsed this, stating evidence is 'compelling' and the manuscript 'provides valuable insights'. Both strongly support the sparse, complementary connectivity model, though OpenEval notes mechanistic claims (C100) lack direct support.

Both address speculative mechanistic proposals about synapse formation and plasticity (C100, C120-C121). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting they are reasonable but lack direct experimental support. Peer reviewers did not explicitly endorse these mechanistic interpretations, accepting them as speculative hypotheses. Both treat these as appropriate future directions rather than supported conclusions.

Both address speculative explanations including comparison with prior models and mechanistic hypotheses (C108-C111). OpenEval rates C110-C111 as UNCERTAIN, noting plausibility but lack of direct testing. Peer reviewers did not explicitly comment on these interpretations. Both implicitly treat the empirical distance threshold as supported while mechanistic explanations remain speculative.

Both address speculative functional interpretations connecting findings to layer function and population representation (C116-C119). OpenEval supports the contextualization with literature but notes functional claims are not tested. Peer reviewers accepted empirical layer differences but did not explicitly endorse functional interpretations. Both treat these as speculative possibilities rather than demonstrated findings.

OpenEval evaluates artifact controls (C47-C50) demonstrating sparse connectivity is not due to edge effects. Peer review R2 addresses the core sparse connectivity findings (C14-C15, C39-C44, C46, C89) which these controls validate. Peer reviewers accepted the sparse connectivity without questioning artifacts, implicitly endorsing the controls. Both support that sparse connectivity is genuine, not artifactual.

OpenEval evaluates vertical organization of connectivity (C51-C53). Peer review R5 addresses layer-specific patterns more broadly (C28-C35, C51-C53, C88). Both include the vertical dispersion findings (C51-C53). Peer reviewers noted 'careful reporting of both columnar and layer position' which encompasses these claims. Both support the vertical organization characterization.

OpenEval evaluates whether synaptic strength contributes to topographic organization (C66-C70). Peer review R4 addresses population-level topography more broadly (C17, C61-C65, C67-C70). Overlap includes C67-C70 showing connectivity patterns dominate over synaptic strength. Both support that topography arises from connectivity patterns rather than synaptic strength gradients.

OpenEval evaluates six validation arguments (C93-C98) supporting genuine sparse connectivity. Peer review R1 addresses methodology validation (C21-C25, C92-C95, C122). Overlap includes C93-C95 about anatomical orientation, layer specificity, and spatial distribution. Both support that findings reflect genuine biology rather than artifacts, though OpenEval provides more comprehensive validation framework.

OpenEval evaluates modeling of input loss due to incomplete sampling (C90-C92). Peer review R1 addresses methodology validation including C92. OpenEval rates this as SUPPORTED but notes modeling details are not fully described. Peer reviewers praised methodology without specifically addressing this limitation. Both accept the <10% input loss estimate as adequate validation.

OpenEval evaluates comparison with Wilson model predictions (C101-C103, C108-C109). Peer review R13 addresses speculative interpretations including C108-C109. OpenEval supports that findings contradict prior predictions. Peer reviewers did not explicitly comment on this comparison. OpenEval provides stronger endorsement of this theoretical advance than peer review explicitly states.

OpenEval evaluates slice preparation validation including EPSC amplitudes (C21-C27, C122). Peer review R8 addresses EPSC amplitudes and inference about presynaptic cell numbers (C26-C27, C98). Both include C26-C27. OpenEval emphasizes these support preparation validity; peer review accepts them as evidence for sparse connectivity. Both support the quantitative measurements.
